pages.title: Editor's Note
pages.content_html:
On the pleasure of turning a page.

We spent the better part of a year asking a simple question: what does a magazine still do that a feed cannot? The answer, repeatedly, was edges. A page ends. A spread resolves. Attention is given a shape.

This issue collects six answers to that question — from a typographer in Lisbon to a bookbinder working out of a converted dairy in Vermont.

pages.title: Letters
pages.content_html:
Readers wrote in about our piece on marginalia. A selection follows.

From Osaka: "I have never once finished a book without arguing with it in pencil."

From Bogotá: "You underrate the humble sticky note."

pages.title: The Weight of Paper
pages.content_html:
Grammage, opacity, and the physics of a satisfying turn.

Paper stock is the invisible protagonist of every printed magazine. Too light and the page flutters; too heavy and the spine fights the reader. Somewhere between 90 and 120 grams per square metre lies a corridor of grace.

Bookbinders call the sound a page makes a riffle. It is measurable: a dry uncoated sheet resonates around two kilohertz, a coated one considerably higher and colder.

The digital analogue of grammage is latency. A page that turns in under eighty milliseconds feels weightless and cheap. Seven hundred milliseconds feels like paper.

pages.title: The Weight of Paper, cont.
pages.content_html:
In Lisbon, a mill has been making the same laid stock since 1908. The watermark is a stork. Nobody at the mill remembers why.

What has changed is the reader. We measured dwell time across three formats and found that the physical spread held attention roughly four times longer than an equivalent scroll — not because the words were better, but because the container promised an ending.

Endings, it turns out, are a feature.

pages.title: Marta Reis on Typographic Silence
pages.content_html:
The Lisbon typographer on white space, restraint, and the tyranny of the headline.

TLF: You describe your work as silence.

MR: A page is mostly not-ink. Designers obsess over the letterforms and forget they are arranging quiet. The reader rests in the quiet.

TLF: And the headline?

MR: A headline should be a doorway, not a shout. If it has to shout, the piece underneath is nervous.

pages.title: Marta Reis, cont.
pages.content_html:
TLF: Does any of this survive a screen?

MR: Of course. A screen is just a page with opinions. What does not survive is infinite length. Silence needs a border to be silent against.

TLF: Last question. Serif or sans?

MR: Both, in their correct rooms.

pages.title: A Dairy Full of Books
pages.content_html:
Vermont, February. A bookbinder named Hollis Ward works where the milk tanks used to be.

The building still smells faintly of cold steel. Ward sews signatures by hand at a bench built from a stanchion rail, then presses them under a screw press older than the barn.

"A book is a hinge," he says. "Everything else is decoration on a hinge."

pages.title: Gallery: Twelve Spines
pages.content_html:
Photographed flat, lit from one side, printed at actual size.

Twelve bindings from the Ward workshop, arranged by the year the leather was tanned. Note the drift in colour: vegetable tanning darkens on a schedule nobody controls.

pages.title: Back Page
pages.content_html:
One last thing.

Our printer leaves a small crop mark on the final sheet of every run. We have asked twice to have it removed. We are glad both times were ignored.
